performers: Odeon Grand Orchestra; conductor disputed (Friedrich Kark / Eduard Künneke)
intro: Odeon’s early recording sends Beethoven’s four-note opening through a horn and onto shellac. The horn calls, violin song and solitary oboe carry a whole orchestral drama across that small surface.

sections.label: A · Three short notes and a hold
sections.mNote: The C-minor opening leads to a violin song in E♭

sections.label: B · The E♭-major closing chords
sections.mNote: Repeated notes bring the exposition to its cadence

sections.label: C · Winds and strings trade single chords
D · The violin song presses towards G
sections.mNote: F♯ leans towards G before the C-major closing group

cues.title: A rest before the blow
cues.text: The famous opening starts with a quaver rest. Then three Gs fall to E♭, held under a fermata; three Fs answer, falling to D. The pauses are as carefully written as the attacks.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, I, bars 1–5; Mutopia 941, first-violin and cello parts.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A melody above repeated notes
cues.text: After the horn call, the first violins sing in E♭ major, marked dolce. The cellos keep returning to three short B♭s and a longer E♭. Beethoven lets the new tune rest on the old rhythm.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 63–70; Mutopia 941, first-violin and cello parts.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Eight sides of Beethoven
cues.text: Odeon issues the complete symphony on eight sides, numbered 76147–76154. The labels name the company orchestra and leave the conductor unnamed. At home, Beethoven’s continuous arguments arrive in portions small enough to fit a disc.
cues.evidence: James Hepokoski, ‘“Listen and Be Amazed!”: Odeon, Künneke, and the First Recordings of Complete Symphonies’, JAMS 76/1 (2023), pp. 113–167, identifies the eight sides, label credits and August 1911 sessions. He attributes the performance to Eduard Künneke; the archive transfer retains the older Kark/1910 identification. https://doi.org/10.1525/jams.2023.76.1.113

cues.title: The strings answer in D♭
cues.text: The horns’ repeated B♭s fall to G. The strings answer with three D♭s and a C, briefly clashing against the held horn note. The opening rhythm starts leading into new keys.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 125–130; Mutopia 941, horns, strings and bassoons.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The rhythm almost disappears
cues.text: Winds and strings exchange single slow chords, with a rest between each reply. Beethoven writes a diminuendo, then asks for still softer playing. The four-note rhythm has dwindled to the barest outline.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 209–227; Mutopia 941, wind and string parts: minim replies, diminuendo, sempre più piano and pp.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: An Adagio for one oboe
cues.text: The orchestra stops after a G-major chord. The oboe continues alone, descending through F, E♭ and D, then turning around the line before another held D. A few notes make a private room inside the symphony.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bar 268; Mutopia 941, oboe solo marked Adagio and accompanying rests.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The call changes players
cues.text: Bassoons take over the earlier horn call. Its new notes, G–G–G–C–D–G, prepare the violin melody in C major. The same tune now sits a minor third lower.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 303–310; Mutopia 941, bassoon and first-violin parts; compare bars 59–66.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: C refuses to settle
cues.text: High C stays in the violins while the bass changes beneath it: C, A♭, E and F. A cadence becomes the start of the coda. The final chords will bring the movement back to C minor.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 374–381 and 491–502; Mutopia 941, strings.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

composer.epithet: He could make a symphony out of four notes, and spent his last years finding things four string players had never said.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. Music was the family trade. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, learning operas from the middle of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was supposed to come back. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him disappeared.
